title: Emotion Beyond Bias: Affective and Cultural Scaffolding in Self-Regulation and Metacognition
abstract: Intelligent performance depends on how cognitive ability is deployed, and its deployment is regulated by metacognitive and affective processes. This theoretical article concerns regulated deployment, on which the gap between maximal and typical performance depends, and leaves the structure of ability outside its scope. Influential decision-science frameworks treat emotion as a bias to be overridden by deliberation and design interventions accordingly; we argue that this view is difficult to reconcile with evidence that emotion and cognition arise from integrated, reciprocally connected networks, and we develop the view that affect functions as an organizing signal for monitoring and control. We derive a hypothesis that, to our knowledge, no study has yet tested directly: for challenges that require regulation to be regenerated over time, or the predictive models from which behavior flows to be reorganized, a culturally mediated route that engages affective, embodied, social, and aesthetic processes should yield change that lasts longer and transfers more widely than a content-matched route without them. We distinguish three classes of behavioral challenge by regulatory structure, locate self-regulated learning and metacognitive calibration within them, separate a testable claim about subjective regulatory effort from a conjecture about the formal control cost of brain-state transitions, and outline a test that could be preregistered.
